prompt: Why combine keyword and vector search rather than picking whichever one benchmarks better?
answer_markdown: Because their failure modes are complementary rather than correlated, so "better on average" hides a permanent blind spot. Vector search is trained to generalise across phrasing, which is precisely wrong for rare exact tokens — an error code, a SKU, a surname, a part number — so the vector for `E4021` sits near the general notion of error codes and chunks merely *about* errors outrank the one chunk containing the literal string. Keyword search has the mirror-image weakness: ask "how do I get my money back" of a document reading "refunds are issued within 14 days" and BM25 scores zero, because no term overlaps. Whichever you pick, you inherit the other's failures forever, and the queries you lose are not the ones your benchmark measured. Running both and fusing the ranked lists gives you a single candidate set that inherits both strengths, which is why hybrid search is close to a default for any corpus containing identifiers.

prompt: What is Reciprocal Rank Fusion, and why does it use ranks instead of the retrievers' scores?
answer_markdown: RRF merges several ranked lists by giving each document `1 / (k + rank)` for every list it appears in and summing those contributions, with `k` conventionally 60 so a single first place cannot dominate the result. It deliberately discards the underlying scores, and that is the whole point: cosine similarity is bounded in 0..1 and clusters in a narrow band, while BM25 is unbounded and its magnitude depends on corpus statistics like term rarity, document length, and tuning constants. A BM25 of 18.4 and a cosine of 0.91 share no common unit, so any scheme that normalises them onto one scale and adds them is inventing a weighting — and that weighting silently shifts every time your corpus grows. Rank position is comparable across any two retrievers by construction, needing no calibration. The useful side effect is that a document ranked well by *both* retrievers beats one ranked brilliantly by only one, which is exactly the judgement you want, since agreement between two independent methods is real evidence of relevance.

prompt: Why retrieve 50 candidates with an embedding search and then rerank, instead of just running the more accurate model over the whole corpus?
answer_markdown: The two models have structurally different costs. The retriever is a bi-encoder: it embedded every chunk once, offline, with no knowledge of any future query, so at query time the chunk vectors already exist and a search is one embedding plus an approximate-nearest-neighbour lookup. That independence is what lets it scan millions of chunks in milliseconds, and also what makes it imprecise, since a single vector must serve every possible question. A cross-encoder instead takes query and chunk together as one input, attending across the pair, so it can notice that the question asks about the Pro tier while this chunk's numbers are the Free tier's. That joint scoring is what makes it accurate and also what makes it impossible to precompute — relevance depends on the pair, so scoring a million chunks means a million forward passes per query. Fifty forward passes is tens of milliseconds; a million is not an option. Hence the standard two-stage shape: stage one optimises recall to get the answer into the candidate set, stage two optimises precision to put it at the top.

prompt: Your RAG answers are wrong but the retrieved chunks look relevant when you read them. How do you diagnose it?
answer_markdown: Stop trusting "looks relevant", because topically similar and actually-contains-the-answer are different properties and the eye conflates them. Build or use a labelled set that maps each failing question to the specific gold chunk that answers it, then check mechanically whether that chunk was retrieved and where it ranked. Three outcomes, three different fixes. If the gold chunk was retrieved and ranked first, the failure is generation — the prompt, the chunk ordering, or the model overriding your context with its training data, which happens most when the retrieved fact is surprising; demand citations and verify every citation resolves to a chunk you actually supplied. If the gold chunk was retrieved but ranked low beneath topically closer distractors, add a cross-encoder reranker over a wider candidate set. If the gold chunk never appeared at all, it is retrieval — chunking split the answer across a boundary, or the query needs hybrid search or decomposition — and no amount of prompt engineering will help. The reason this triage is possible at all is that you measured retrieval separately from generation; a single end-to-end quality score cannot distinguish these cases, and would have sent you to tune chunk size when the problem was the prompt.

prompt: You are switching to a new embedding model. What has to happen?
answer_markdown: You must re-embed the entire corpus, because two embedding models learn unrelated coordinate systems during their own training runs — dimension 7 in one has no relationship to dimension 7 in the other, even when the dimension counts match. There is no incremental migration and no mixed index: comparing a vector from model A against one from model B computes perfectly, returns a plausible-looking number in the normal 0.6–0.9 band, and is meaningless, with nothing in your logs saying so. Operationally, do it behind a blue/green index alias. The application always reads through an alias rather than a concrete index name, so you build the new index alongside the old one, backfill it completely, verify recall@k on your golden set against the old index's numbers before cutting over, then repoint the alias atomically — and roll back by repointing again if the numbers regressed. Queries must switch to the new model at the same instant the alias moves, since a query embedded by the old model against the new index is exactly the silent-failure case. The same procedure applies to any chunking change, because re-chunking also changes the vectors.

prompt: How do you stop one tenant's users retrieving another tenant's documents?
answer_markdown: Enforce it as a metadata filter applied inside the vector search — tenant id, ACL, document classification — so an ineligible chunk is never a candidate in the first place. Filtering after retrieval is not equivalent and not safe: the index has already ranked documents the user cannot see, so your top 50 becomes a handful of survivors drawn from the wrong 50, and the chunks the user was actually entitled to were never scored. Crucially, do not put the documents in the prompt and instruct the model to withhold them — that is a request, not an access control, and it fails to anyone who asks in the right way. This matters more in RAG than intuition suggests because embeddings are good: the same policy document for two different tenants is near-identical in meaning, so the two copies sit almost on top of each other in vector space and their similarity scores differ by noise. No threshold can separate them; only a predicate can.

prompt: When is RAG the wrong tool for the job?
answer_markdown: Three cases. First, when the knowledge is small and stable enough to fit in the context window — put it in the prompt and cache the prefix, because a retrieval pipeline you do not need is infrastructure, extra latency, and a new failure mode bought for nothing. Second, when the problem is behaviour or output format rather than facts: "always answer in this JSON shape" or "adopt our house style" cannot be taught by retrieving passages, and belongs to prompting first and fine-tuning second. Third, and most commonly missed, when the question requires aggregating over the whole corpus rather than reading a few passages. "How many contracts expire this year?" cannot be answered from five retrieved chunks, because retrieval returns passages and does not count; the right answer is a query over structured data — text-to-SQL or a precomputed metric. Recognising this third case matters in interviews, because a candidate who proposes RAG for an aggregation question has revealed they are pattern-matching on "questions about documents" rather than thinking about what retrieval actually returns.
